title: The Urban Heat Island — Practice Set

items.prompt: What is the main point of the passage?

options.text: Cities are warmer than rural areas because the global mean temperature is rising rapidly.
The urban heat island is a measurable local effect produced by built surfaces and human activity, and its costs fall unevenly on residents.
Planting trees and lightening surfaces will solve the heat problem within a single season.
Heat waves are mainly caused by the expansion of suburban housing estates.

items.explanation: The passage moves from defining and measuring the island, through its physical mechanisms, to who is exposed and what governance can do. It neither attributes the effect solely to global warming (A), nor promises a seasonal fix (C, which the final paragraph explicitly denies).

items.prompt: According to the passage, when is the urban excess at its most pronounced?

options.text: On still, clear summer nights in the urban core.
On extreme summer afternoons in subtropical megacities.
During daytime in rural areas with tall grass.
Immediately after heavy rainfall in industrial zones.

items.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that comparisons are usually made on still, clear nights, when the contrast is at its most pronounced. B is a different measurement (surface temperature in subtropical megacities) and the passage notes that surface contrasts matter less for comfort than air temperature.

items.prompt: Which of the following is NOT identified in the passage as a cause of the urban heat island?

options.text: Low albedo of paving and roofing materials.
Absence of evapotranspiration over impermeable surfaces.
The trapping of long-wave radiation between buildings and streets.
The combustion of fossil fuels in distant power stations.

items.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists low albedo, lack of evapotranspiration and the trapping of long-wave radiation as the three physical mechanisms. Distant power stations are not mentioned; the anthropogenic heat named in paragraph 4 is discharged locally into the street canyon.

items.prompt: What do models that remove anthropogenic heat but keep the city geometry unchanged show?

options.text: The heat island disappears entirely, proving human activity is the only cause.
A substantial nighttime excess remains, so built form alone can produce the island.
Temperatures in the core fall below the rural baseline.
Daytime surface temperatures rise even further.

items.explanation: Paragraph 4: the models 'still report a substantial nighttime excess', and the author concludes that built form alone is sufficient to produce an island while human activity amplifies it.

items.prompt: Why does the author say that plans assuming a uniform city temperature mis-allocate assistance?

options.text: Because the hottest districts are also the smallest and hold the most concentrated people at risk.
Because rural areas need almost no assistance during heat waves.
Because hospitals cannot record admissions reliably.
Because most residents move out of the core in summer.

items.explanation: Paragraph 6 gives the reason directly: people most at risk are concentrated in 'the smallest and hottest parts of the metropolitan area'. B and C are unsupported; D reverses the commuting pattern described.

items.prompt: Nighttime temperatures inside dense urban cores can exceed those of outlying neighbourhoods by several degrees under identical weather conditions.

options.text: TRUE
FALSE
NOT GIVEN

items.explanation: Paragraph 1 states exactly this: the excess appears 'even when both share the same latitude, altitude and weather system'.

items.prompt: Surface temperature differences between urban and rural terrain are the most reliable guide to the heat that residents actually experience.

options.text: TRUE
FALSE
NOT GIVEN

items.explanation: Paragraph 2 says surface contrasts 'matter less for human comfort than the air that people actually breathe', so the claim reverses the passage's ordering. TRUE/FALSE is given because the passage explicitly addresses the point.

items.prompt: Giving off anthropogenic heat is the only cause of the urban heat island.

options.text: TRUE
FALSE
NOT GIVEN

items.explanation: Paragraphs 3 and 4 establish three physical mechanisms plus anthropogenic heat as a fourth, independent contribution; models without anthropogenic heat still show an excess. The passage addresses the point directly, so it is ruled false rather than unstated.

items.prompt: People without air conditioning in older housing and with little nearby tree cover take in the largest share of excess heat.

options.text: TRUE
FALSE
NOT GIVEN

items.explanation: Paragraph 5 names old housing stock without air conditioning, informal settlements with little canopy and neighbourhoods beside traffic or industry as receiving 'the largest dose'.

items.prompt: A newly planted street tree provides its full cooling effect within the first summer.

options.text: TRUE
FALSE
NOT GIVEN

items.explanation: The final paragraph says tree planting 'needs decades to reach canopy maturity, whereas heat waves arrive within a single season'. Ruled false because the passage addresses the timescale directly.

options.text: the ability of a surface to store water for later release
the proportion of incoming solar radiation a surface reflects
the rate at which a material releases stored heat at night
the depth of soil available to plant roots

items.explanation: The passage explains the term by its consequence: materials with low albedo 'absorb a large share of incoming solar radiation', so a low albedo means a small reflected proportion (B).

options.text: the slow oxidation of organic matter in soil
the combined evaporation of water from soil and its transpiration through plants
the condensation of vapour on building surfaces at night
the circulation of air between streets and rooftops

items.explanation: Paragraph 3 glosses the term directly as 'a process that impermeable surfaces cannot perform', following the mention of trees and soils cooling their surroundings. B is the standard definition.

items.prompt: In paragraph 3, "impermeable" is used to describe surfaces that

options.text: allow no liquid or gas to pass through
absorb large quantities of heat quickly
reflect most incoming radiation
drain water towards underground reservoirs

items.explanation: In context the word contrasts with soil and vegetation, which cool through evaporation; the intended meaning is that paved surfaces cannot pass water or air through, hence cannot support evapotranspiration.

items.prompt: In paragraph 6, how is "compounds" most likely to be read?

options.text: To make a difficulty worse or more severe
To add the numbers of two quantities together
To break a substance into smaller chemical units
To agree with a proposal at a meeting

items.explanation: The sentence is 'Population mobility compounds the difficulty', followed by the reason (commuters are exposed in the core). None of the other readings fits a difficulty as the object; only making it worse does.

items.prompt: In the final paragraph, "regulatory floor" refers to

options.text: the lowest temperature below which no further action is required
a mandatory minimum standard written into rules for new development
the price floor set for land in the suburban housing market
the minimum level of funding the city must reserve each year

items.explanation: The parenthetical gloss explains it as 'minimum canopy cover and maximum impermeable surface in new development', i.e. a binding standard in regulation, not a temperature or a price limit.
